content: Many hospitalized patients experience medication errors (MEs), which can lead to discomfort, harm, or even death. Children are particularly vulnerable to harm from MEs because such errors pose greater risks to them compared to adults. Despite efforts to reduce MEs, interventions implemented so far have only achieved limited success. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions designed to reduce MEs and associated harm in hospitalized children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search for primary studies was conducted by the Effective Practice and Organisation of Care (EPOC) Group Trials Search Coordinator. The search included databases such as The Cochrane Library (including CENTRAL, EED, and HTA), MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, ProQuest Dissertations & Theses, Web of Science, and the EPOC Register of Studies. Additional sources, including grey literature, trial registries, selected journals, and reference lists of relevant reviews, were also examined. Searches were conducted in November 2013 and November 2014, with no restrictions on language or publication date. The review included randomized controlled trials, controlled before-and-after studies, and interrupted time series that investigated interventions aimed at improving medication safety in hospitalized children aged 18 years or younger. The participants in these studies were healthcare professionals authorized to prescribe, dispense, or administer medications. The outcomes assessed included the frequency of MEs, potential or actual patient harm, resource utilization, and unintended consequences of the interventions. Two independent reviewers selected the studies, extracted data, and assessed the quality of the included studies using the EPOC data collection checklist. The risk of bias was evaluated, and the GRADE approach was used to assess the overall quality of the evidence. The results were described narratively and summarized in GRADE tables. Seven studies were included in the review, describing five different types of interventions. These interventions were: the involvement of a clinical pharmacist in the clinical team (two studies), the implementation of a computerized physician order entry (CPOE) system (two studies), the use of a barcode medication administration system (one study), the introduction of a structured prescribing form (one study), and the implementation of a check-and-control checklist combined with feedback (one study). Due to clinical and methodological differences between the studies, meta-analyses could not be performed. While some interventions demonstrated a reduction in MEs, the results were inconsistent, and none of the studies showed a significant reduction in patient harm. According to the GRADE approach, the overall quality and strength of the evidence were determined to be low. In conclusion, the current evidence on effective interventions to prevent MEs in hospitalized children is limited. There is a need for comparative studies with robust designs to evaluate interventions that specifically address pediatric safety concerns.
